articles.title: Congress drifts toward shutdown deadline without a funding strategy
articles.summary: Congress has less than a month before the deadline to fund the government, and neither party has coalesced around a battle strategy for what’s almost certain to be a testy fight. Republicans still have the majority until January, but they have moved slowly on full-year spending bills, meaning they only have a handful of weeks…
articles.body:
Congress has less than a month before the deadline to fund the government, and neither party has coalesced around a battle strategy for what’s almost certain to be a testy fight.

Republicans still have the majority until January, but they have moved slowly on full-year spending bills, meaning they only have a handful of weeks to fund the government through the traditional appropriations process.

Avoiding a government shutdown will require some kind of bipartisan agreement by Dec. 11, when the current continuing resolution (CR) expires.

Republicans on the Senate Appropriations Committee said there are still lots of moving pieces, but the end result is likely going to be some kind of short-term CR.

What will be in it, and whether Democrats will get on board, are open questions. The government’s operations hang in the balance.

“Everybody’s talking about a continuing resolution,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.). “And it may be a resolution with some anomalies to it. That’ll depend, but I’m not hearing anybody talking about actually getting the appropriation bills done at this stage of the game, other than a continuing resolution until sometime in February or March. It’s just the reality of where we’re at today.”

Other GOP senators said their ideal would be to pass the full-year appropriations bills, but they think the more realistic outcome is that those bills will either form a framework of a CR, or a hybrid short-term package that includes some of the noncontroversial long-term bills, known as a “cromnibus.”

“We’ve started posting the bills, and if you do a CR, those will be the basis in the sense that those are bills that both sides have worked on very hard,” said Sen. John Boozman (R-Ark.). “As far as actually getting CR language down, not yet. What you have to do is have some kind of an omnibus, ‘cromnibus’ taking some of them, maybe passing some others.”

Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.) told reporters Wednesday evening she’s in favor of working through full-year bills while Republicans are still in power in the remainder of the year, rather than a blank short-term CR.

“We’re still going to give appropriations a try, I think … anytime we pass a CR, it costs taxpayers more,” Britt said. “So we’re committed to trying that again when we get back.”

Rep. Tom Cole (R-Okla.), chair of the House Appropriations Committee, said in a statement Wednesday that he’s still gunning for those longer-term bills before the end of the year.

“A lame-duck doesn’t have to leave full-year bills dead in the water,” Cole said. “I’ve been actively working with my counterparts to advance negotiations, avoid an unnecessary shutdown, and get full-year FY [fiscal year] 27 legislation signed into law. The biggest disservice to the American people would be not to try.”

Meanwhile, a group of Democrats are preparing to use any leverage at their disposal to pass a measure that would force President Trump to end the war in Iran. They’re looking at the likely CR as a potential avenue to amend accordingly.

Democratic Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.), Tammy Duckworth (Ill.) and Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) announced Wednesday that they’ll attach an amendment to “any proposed funding bill” barring any funds from being used for the war. Other Democrats have already said language restricting funding for the war is a must-have for them on any short-term funding patch.

But it’s not clear whether a majority of Democrats will insist on such an addition before getting to yes.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro (Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, told reporters Wednesday she is in favor of passing the full-year spending bills, at least for as many uncontroversial funding priorities as possible, and a “short” CR to extend other funding. She added there’s no CR text yet.

DeLauro also did not commit to holding up funding priorities to bankrupt Trump’s war against Iran but cautioned against shutting the government down over such a move.

“I’m sure there’s some who have that appetite,” she said. “My view is that what further puts our forward-looking agenda in jeopardy is for a government to shut down.”

In the meantime, Republicans were hoping to move forward on a reconciliation package, which only needs Republican support and could be used to beef up defense spending, which Democrats are not likely to do when they retake the majority in both chambers in January.

Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) said amidst reconciliation talks that passing a defense-focused bill could smooth government funding because it would remove the most controversial obstacle to bipartisan consensus.

Besides some wanting a ban on funding the Iran war, Democrats also want a broader appropriations agreement that balances defense spending with spending on domestic priorities like infrastructure and healthcare. The stalemate over that balance has been ongoing for months.

Hoeven said that Republicans passing their own defense package could solve both problems.

“They want to hold up defense, right? And if we just do that through reconciliation, takes it off the table,” Hoeven said. “Then, other than just wanting to shut down the government, what are they holding up funding anymore for?”

But later on Wednesday, Republicans emerged from a meeting to discuss reconciliation with a more tepid view, saying it was still an option but they’d prefer a negotiated bipartisan product to boost defense spending.

“Before we go directly into reconciliation, let’s find out whether or not there is any possibility at all of finding a supplemental and addressing the issues that our Democrat colleagues have got, and a way to show good support for our troops,” Rounds told reporters after the meeting.

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), whose committee would lead any reconciliation push, told reporters “probably not this week” when asked after the meeting what the latest talks meant for reconciliation.

“But again, we’re not taking it off the table at all,” Johnson said.

articles.title: The Memo: Trump administration fails to quell concern over cascade of tech outages
articles.summary: The Trump administration is not out of the woods yet on the knotty issues of cybersecurity, AI threats and creaky tech infrastructure — even though almost a week has gone by since the nation’s longest air traffic ground stop in a quarter-century. The hours-long collapse of the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) air traffic control system…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is not out of the woods yet on the knotty issues of cybersecurity, AI threats and creaky tech infrastructure — even though almost a week has gone by since the nation’s longest air traffic ground stop in a quarter-century.

The hours-long collapse of the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) air traffic control system last Friday was just the most dramatic moment amid a cascade of tech failures.

Outages, disruptions and malfunctions have hit other branches of government, such as the National Security Agency, and have affected some of the biggest brand names in American commerce, including Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and United Airlines.

The White House and its allies have tried to tamp down the problems. President Trump himself declared, “It’s fine.”

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen,” Trump told reporters near the start of his Asia trip.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in the Philippines on Wednesday, told reporters there was “zero evidence” that the various incidents “are related to each other.”

Rubio also insisted there was no reason to believe the occurrences “have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyberhackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind.”

But even some usually loyal Republicans have seemed unpersuaded.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told reporters at the Capitol on Tuesday that the full Senate ought to be briefed on the issue.

Referring to the official explanation for the air traffic control meltdown, Hawley said, “Maybe it’s because, you know, somebody unplugged a router in Arkansas or whatever. I dunno. I find that, frankly, a little hard to believe.”

More generally, Hawley admitted he was not sure what was going on.

“If this is all coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world. You can’t tell me that all of this just is happenstance,” he said.

To be sure, there are some challenges inherent to the situation that any administration would struggle to overcome.

For example, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has been candid about the fact that the precise cause of the air traffic outage has not been identified, even though it appears to have something to do with an upgrade and a router.

But there have been avoidable stumbles, too — including somewhat different messages from different members of the administration.

At a hastily convened White House press conference last Friday, just after the ground stop had lifted, Duffy appeared to dissent as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin spoke about what caused the issue.

“What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment, new technology was overwhelming the older system,” Mullin said. Duffy, standing alongside him, looked down and shook his head.

Mullin also caused some consternation earlier this week when he cited an unnamed “one guy that’s very smart with tech” as the source of insight during an interview with Fox News.

This person, whom Mullin said was not Elon Musk, apparently contended that the root of the problem was the difficulty in making older software work in combination with the turbo-charged capabilities of artificial intelligence.

Beyond the specifics of Mullin’s performance, even some GOP-friendly voices express concern about the White House’s messaging.

At various times, Trump, Rubio, Duffy, Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton have all spoken publicly about the matter.

“They really need one person to be the communications lead and they need one clear message,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist who is also the CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI. “As they get more facts, they can share those facts — and avoiding speculation as much as possible is a good thing. But we have got quite a few different messages.”

A consistent and reassuring message, Steinhauser added, was especially important on issues like cyberthreats and AI, which are evolving at warp speed and seem ominous to broad swathes of the public — even as the minutiae of how the technology works remains opaque to most people.

“The American people’s fears are rational,” he asserted. “We are entering a new era where things are going to get worse because AI is going to transform everything … Defensive capabilities are not going to keep up with offensive capabilities, so we are going to have a lot of instability in our critical infrastructure.”

The public’s nerves are frayed further because the spate of recent developments is taking place against a backdrop of the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and the broader challenge the U.S. faces from China.

Indeed, even as all the outages have been taking place, Nvidia — for a period the world’s most highly-valued company — has been roiled by the departure of its CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang amid allegations that a woman with whom he had an affair was a Chinese agent.

China denies this, and the woman, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen Huang — has not spoken publicly about the matter.

In terms of the outages themselves, a senior administration official told reporters on a Wednesday morning call that the precise causes were “disparate” but “in the upgrading and patching realm.”

But those statements don’t assuage the concerns — both technological and political — of those who fear that Trump’s tendency toward ebullient rhetoric is disconnected from public concerns.

“I don’t know what this president truly feels, but he certainly has not shown an appetite to talk about the dangers in a way that many voters would like to hear,” said GOP strategist Dan Judy.

“I think what most voters want is to be reassured that some adults in the room are keeping tabs on this — and I don’t think that’s what this administration is going for.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Democrats worry Van Hollen’s hard-line Iran stance could trigger shutdown
articles.summary: Senate Democrats are pushing back on Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) call to insist on adding language to any government funding bill to immediately end the Iran war, warning that stumbling into a government shutdown before the holidays would be a disastrous move. Van Hollen’s demand to use government funding as leverage to shut down…
articles.body:
Senate Democrats are pushing back on Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) call to insist on adding language to any government funding bill to immediately end the Iran war, warning that stumbling into a government shutdown before the holidays would be a disastrous move.

Van Hollen’s demand to use government funding as leverage to shut down the 8 1/2-month military conflict with Iran is popular with the Democratic Party’s activist base, but Democratic colleagues in the Senate are pumping the brakes on taking a hard-line stance that could risk a shutdown.

The vast majority of Democratic senators, including Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.), whom Van Hollen is challenging, want to end the war immediately.

But they’re leery about overplaying their leverage ahead of the Dec. 11 government funding deadline.

After picking up nine Senate seats with Mary Peltola’s projected victory in Alaska and 43 House seats, Democrats on Capitol Hill want to avoid a potential shutdown they fear could derail their agenda ahead of taking control of both chambers in January.

“Nobody I’ve talked to thinks a shutdown makes any sense,” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) said.

Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) warned “a shutdown of government right before the holidays is a tough nut.”

He called a shutdown a “dire situation” but said the Iran war has dragged on for months, and voters sent a clear message to Washington in this month’s election that they want the conflict resolved.

Hickenlooper declined to endorse Van Hollen’s call to insist on adding a rider to the funding stopgap that needs to pass by Dec. 11 that would block any appropriated funding from supporting the military conflict with Iran.

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) said Democrats “need to avoid a government shutdown” while finding a way to wind down the war as soon as possible.

“It is vital that we stay strong on bringing this war to a conclusion. It is vital that we fund the government and that’s the balance that we’re trying to find,” he said.

Van Hollen joined three Senate colleagues last week in a joint statement that called on Democratic leaders to insist that any short-term government funding deal includes “language that restricts the Trump administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

Sens. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) joined the statement.

Senate Republicans are warning that stance will likely trigger another government shutdown — the third in just more than a year.

“I’m increasingly concerned that the Democrats may try to initiate another — a third — government shutdown this year and that would be a terrible outcome for the American people,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said.

“We do not need — we’ve already had two long, extended government shutdowns. We saw the impact that has on the American people. The American people don’t need another government shutdown. We need to make sure that people are getting paid,” he said.

Thune called Van Hollen’s demand to add language to any funding stopgap to prohibit any funding for the war “short-sighted.”

“They’re going to have the majorities, they’re going to have the gavels next year. I don’t know why you’d force another government shutdown,” he said. “That’s not a realistic ask. I understand he may be in the middle of a political campaign and feels compelled to do something like that, but it’s not good for the country.”

A Senate Republican aide warned a shutdown could drag into 2027 and that Democrats might find it very hard to reopen federal departments or agencies once they take control of Congress next year.

The GOP aide also warned that triggering a shutdown could cause travel havoc ahead of Christmas, noting the 43-day government shutdown caused problems at airports after air traffic controllers began missing work after not getting paid for several weeks.

Van Hollen’s bid to oust Schumer from leadership and his call for Democrats to take an aggressive stance on defense funding, however, are winning plaudits from progressive advocates.

He received a standing ovation from a room full of progressive donors, union leaders and movement leaders at the Democracy Alliance conference in Washington on Wednesday, according to a person who was in the room.

Schumer, who is viewed as the favorite in the race to become Senate majority leader, said Congress should use its “power of the purse” to end the war. But he has spoken more generally about that goal.

“We’re going to end the war. … The Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” Schumer said at a press conference on the day after Election Day.

Senate Democrats discussed their strategy for the approaching Dec. 11 government funding deadline at a caucus lunch meeting on Tuesday.

Several Democrats called for finding a way to reach a funding compromise with Republicans to limit funding for the war without putting Congress at risk of stumbling into another shutdown.

“Everybody in our caucus believes that we should not be spending any more money to support the war and everybody in our caucus believes that we want to figure how to pass the CR. There ought to be a way for doing both of those things,” said a Democratic senator who requested anonymity to talk about internal discussions, referring to a continuing resolution to fund the government.

The Democratic senator said forcing a shutdown to end the war is a “ridiculous choice.”

“There’s no automatic reason that the only way to not fund the war is to have the government go into shutdown. That’s a ridiculous choice and that’s not the choice,” they added. “That’s what we’re talking about.

“Everybody is pretty realistic,” the lawmaker continued.

Van Hollen spoke up at Tuesday’s Democratic caucus meeting to defend his position. He argued that Democrats heard a clear call from voters to use their power to end the war now, according to a source familiar with the meeting.

A second person familiar with the meeting, however, said Van Hollen did not go so far as to argue that Democrats should risk a government shutdown to cut off funding for the conflict.

articles.title: 'Frustrated' - Democrats remain a divided party despite winning big in midterms
articles.summary: After winning power in Congress, a Democratic conference in Denver was animated with talk on the best way forward.
articles.body:
When James Talarico - who recently became the first Democrat to win election to the US Senate for Texas since 1988 - appeared onstage at a Democratic political conference, he was greeted by a chorus of cheers and a standing ovation.

But the audience's enthusiasm dimmed when he suggested working in tandem with the Republican Trump administration.

"We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history," said Talarico, who at 37 will become the youngest member of the Senate when he takes his oath of office in January. "Because this moment is so much bigger and so much more important than the red team or the blue team."

He was just one of many rising stars speaking last week during a political conference in Denver, titled "What's Next: investigating strategies and priorities for the future of the Democratic Party".

And the answer to what's next? No one's sure.

Those present, who included activists and political organisers, were invigorated and celebratory the week after a "blue tsunami" saw Democrats win in Republican heartlands in the midterm elections.

The party took control of both chambers of Congress, winning a majority in the House by over 80 seats and gaining nine seats in the Senate.

But the atmosphere in Denver was also introspective and forward-looking, as discussions focused on how those victories were won, which issues did not resonate, and what would be needed to continue the party's seat-winning momentum.

Some, like Talarico, suggested working alongside Republicans to push forward an economic agenda that would resonate with Americans, such as extending health coverage and reducing inflation.

Alabama Congressman Shomari Figures - who surprised many pollsters when he held his seat despite Republicans redrawing his district months before the election - cautioned against going after Trump, when there were more pressing concerns for Americans.

Previous Democratic-led efforts to impeach Trump both ended in Senate acquittals.

"We impeached him twice and got him back - with a Republican majority," Figures said.

Yet others, like Maryland Congresswoman Angela Alsobrooks, insisted that voters wanted to see accountability.

Voters "realised the smash-and-grab that occurred, and they want people to account for it", she said, pushing for transparent investigations into the Trump administration.

The two-day event was staged by Majority Democrats, a political action committee launched last year to address tensions between the left and centrist factions of the party, with some of the biggest divisions forming over how to deliver health care and the war in Gaza.

Prominent left-wing members of the party - such as Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed - were not in attendance.

In Denver, it was clear those tensions weren't going away, as protesters waving Palestinian flags shouted as people walked past and armed police looked on.

Some in attendance made a point to criticise Chuck Schumer, the long-time Democratic Senate minority leader who is seen as a part of the party's centrist establishment.

He has been challenged for the role of Senate majority leader by Chris Van Hollen, a senator from Maryland who is considered a left-wing populist.

Democrats have not been "strong enough in their displeasure with what's been happening with Trump, and I think that's one of the reasons that people are asking for new leadership," said Vicki Saxe, holding a sign criticising Schumer.

"I'm frustrated with the lack of urgency that I feel coming from the party leadership," said Tami Butters, 65, standing beside her with a "Vote Yes for Chris Van Hollen" sign. She cited the absence of 11 Democrats last week, when the House voted on whether to consider impeaching US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The effort failed.

Hakeem Jeffries, a centrist Democrat who is poised to become the country's first black speaker of the House, faced similar pushback, as protesters heckled his speech.

One of the biggest issues of division is the war in Gaza, with both Schumer and Jeffries backing continued military assistance for Israel, while some new members of Congress, like El-Sayed, support ending unconditional US military aid to Israel.

Non-profit founder Shiva Saram, who also chairs the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, travelled from Connecticut to the conference despite having "almost left my party over Gaza and the Iran War".

Saram has been newly encouraged, however, by the "real depth in our bench of new and young leaders".

"What my party has done wrong for too long is we did not listen," she said.

Many speakers and guests stressed that the Democrats won because they focused on real policies that would impact their constituents' daily lives - and that failing to do so in previous years might have been why they lost on those occasions.

Delaware Senator Chris Coons told BBC News that he had advised newly elected members to "under-promise and over-deliver".

"We got hired because the average American wants us to help make their lives better - lower their costs, end the cruelty and the corruption and give them more reason for hope," he said. "That's going to require hard work, and it isn't going to be easy to get done."

Michigan Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet agreed, saying she did not care "if we have to put Donald Trump's name" on legislation to gain the president's support for efforts to help her district.

Tahra Hoops, the 28-year-old senior director of economic analysis at the Chamber of Progress, a "left-of-centre" tech think tank, suggested that the party's divisions be embraced, not paved over.

"I think Democrats can look different wherever they are," she said.

While "very progressive" candidates can win in her home town of New York City, she said it made sense that Talarico held more centrist views because running in Texas "is not going to be the same".

"America is a very diverse country; our politicians and their views should also be diverse," she added.

Carlos Repetto-Ayala, a campaign consultant, made a similar point. The 25-year-old Texan travelled with two friends to the What's Next? event, wearing a cowboy hat and a red-white-and-blue pin on his lapel in the shape of the Lone Star State.

"It is a big tent party, but I think, as long as everyone that's in the party is laser-focused on addressing the issues that people would like for them to fix, I think Democrats will be successful," he said.

articles.title: With Kerch bridge strike, Zelensky shows he isn’t asking Trump’s permission any more
articles.summary: Ukraine’s first major attack on the Kerch Strait Bridge was delivered by a truck bomb in October 2022, followed by strikes using unmanned surface vessels, S-200 rockets, and underwater explosives placed near pillars supporting the bridge. This week, the Ukrainians finally finished the job. As President Volodymyr Zelensky described it in a post on X, the operation surrounding the new strike had been…
articles.body:
Ukraine’s first major attack on the Kerch Strait Bridge was delivered by a truck bomb in October 2022, followed by strikes using unmanned surface vessels , S-200 rockets , and underwater explosives placed near pillars supporting the bridge.

This week, the Ukrainians finally finished the job.

As President Volodymyr Zelensky described it in a post on X , the operation surrounding the new strike had been “carried out over several weeks, developed and coordinated by the Security Service of Ukraine together with the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Our warriors gradually destroyed air defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective.”

Recall how, in February 2025, Trump lectured Zelensky in the Oval Office: “You’re not in a good position. You don’t have the cards right now.”

As of Tuesday, Zelensky had the cards. And he had given his own kinetic answer to President Trump and his envoys regarding their chosen path proposal on Tuesday: He would not let Trump’s meeting today with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin become Yalta 2.0 , in which his country is divided up behind his back.

Last May when CNN’s Jim Sciutto interviewed Ukraine’s Ambassador to the U.S. Olha Stefanishyna’s , he asked her, “Is it safe to say Ukraine does have cards in this conflict?”

Her response was priceless: “We printed them. … We made our own.”

That they did. According to Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara , “The [Kerch] strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons — using our technologies and our solutions.”

Zelensky confirmed that domestically manufactured missiles and drones were used on both the road and rail sections of the bridge. That created an awkward backdrop for Trump’s meeting last night with Xi Jinping and Putin in Shenzhen.

The more Trump’s negotiation team has tried to advance its agenda, the more Zelensky has pushed back. And Zelensky has paid a price: His Starshield defense network service was throttled. His access to Patriot missiles was diminished . Yet he has fought the Russians to a standstill. And the Kerch Bridge attack may signal that the tide is turning in his favor. He is not about to abandon the Donbas region in exchange for promises of lucrative deals or economic opportunities .

For Ukraine and for Europe, national security takes precedence over both oil and mineral riches. As German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned during his visit to Kyiv in October, “If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later.”

The White House must adopt a different course of action. Instead of trying to make Ukraine quit, he should defund Russia. Waiving sanctions and seeking economic opportunities with Russia only keeps the Kremlin’s war machine going.

The White House must join Europe and enable Kyiv to defeat the Kremlin’s remaining source of power — aerial attacks.

Trump claims he wants to stop the killing. To date, Putin’s special military operation has yielded 1,629,010 Russian casualties — more than 54,000 in October alone . In the first 15 days of November, the Kremlin sustained on average 2,343 casualties per day — 35,145 casualties, nearly twice the number of Russian soldiers killed in its 10- year war with Afghanistan , and on pace for 70,000 by month’s end.

The best way to stop the killing is not to force Ukraine to give up — rather, it is to get Russia to stop attacking.

The Kremlin is displaying a false confidence of victory, with senior officials telling Putin-aligned lawmakers to “ prepare for victory ” in Ukraine. We have seen that before. In April 2022, as they drove the Russians back from their initial thrust toward Kyiv, Ukrainian forces found parade uniforms in their abandoned baggage. They thought they would be celebrating a victory within days of their invasion.

When Zelensky’s request for ammo fell short, he simply made his own and stopped asking permission. Persistence, resilience, adaptation and continued support from those still fully willing made Tuesday’s strike possible.

Needless to say, U.S. mediated trilateral negotiations are probably off the table in the near term. But there will be a Russian response, and the targets will likely be Ukrainian civilians in their homes. Kyiv will need to get its home-grown anti-ballistic missile defense system into the field sooner rather than later.

Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy They are the co-founders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: China blocks Bloomberg reporter from Trump-Putin-Xi meeting over question to Trump
articles.summary: Chinese officials barred Bloomberg's Annmarie Hordern from the meeting of President Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin after her earlier question.
articles.body: Chinese officials barred a Bloomberg reporter from a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin after she asked a question during an earlier bilateral session. The clash over press access unfolded on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China, where the three leaders gathered for their first-ever three-way meeting to discuss nuclear arms control, trade and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Despite a push from the White House to get her admitted, Chinese officials refused to budge on barring Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern from the room. Hordern was blocked after she called out a question to Trump during his earlier one-on-one meeting with Xi: "President Trump, has Jensen Huang been disloyal to the United States?" CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO A second reporter also started to ask a question during the bilateral session but was shushed by Chinese officials. Beijing subsequently passed along a message to the U.S. travel pool warning that yelling questions is considered "extremely rude" and that journalists would be pulled from the room if they did so. A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity surrounding the issue, said Chinese officials insisted Hordern not be allowed into the trilateral meeting even as the White House advocated for her inclusion. TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS The dispute over press rules stood out alongside the friendly tone Trump sought to project toward both leaders during the summit. Trump praised his friendship with Xi, who greeted Air Force One on the tarmac Wednesday with a one-armed hug and called Putin "my friend" ahead of a separate 40-minute sit-down. Tensions over artificial intelligence, however, still hung over the meetings. articles.title: Trump meets with ‘friends’ Xi, Putin: ‘We are really making history’
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Trump wraps up China summit ▪ Officials grilled over outages ▪ House Democrats show unity ▪ Closer U.S.-Venezuela partnership President Trump is on his way back home following a multi-day trip to Asia capped off by face-to-face meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump met separately…
articles.body:
President Trump is on his way back home following a multi-day trip to Asia capped off by face-to-face meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin .

Trump met separately with Putin and with Xi before all three world leaders engaged in trilateral talks, which were set to focus on the issue of nuclear nonproliferation.

The president had warm words for his fellow leaders before and after the meetings, which is sure to rankle critics who are uneasy about Trump’s closeness to two dictators.

“I’m delighted that this trip has also given us the opportunity for this first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China, and today, so in that sense, and I think in lots of other ways, we are really making history,” Trump said of the meeting.

“Our three nations are united not only by the status of victors in the Second World War but mainly by our responsibility for maintaining international peace,” Putin said.

Trump referred to Putin as his “friend” and touted their “great” relationship, adding that he expected much to come out of their meeting. He made similar comments about Xi, thanking him for an “incredible warm welcome” and praising their “outstanding personal relationship.”

Xi broke precedent on Wednesday when he personally greeted Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia Pacific Economic Forum (APEC) summit. Giving Trump an uncharacteristic hug, Xi reciprocated Trump’s gesture upon his visit to the U.S. in September.

The gestures and kind words have been received with a mixed reaction from members of Trump’s party, who largely support Trump meeting with them but caution they are “not our friends,” The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports .

Trump defended his closeness with his fellow leaders and willingness to meet with them, saying they have a responsibility to keep an open dialogue.

“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite,” he said. “I think that we are sure about that.”

Trump focused on one issue Xi has shown little interest in — placing limits on the number of nuclear weapons. Ahead of the meeting, the White House had downplayed the chances of a breakthrough.

“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said.

“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard not to have them,” he added.

Xi aid nuclear weapons should be “completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time” and countries should comply with the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

“On major sensitive issues concerning one another, it is important to communicate in advance, try to see things from one another’s perspective, act with caution, and in particular, not to challenge the red lines of one another,” Xi said, according to Chinese state media.

The three leaders issued a “peace declaration” consisting of four points following the meeting. They agreed to promote U.N. reforms so the organization can respond more effectively to global challenges, increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, that the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies should not “abuse” their jurisdiction and that a nuclear war must not be fought.

Trump and Putin have been particular critics of the ICC as the institution has issued arrest warrants for Putin for his conduct in the Ukraine war and for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , a close Trump ally, over the war in Gaza.

Trump also said the war in Ukraine would be discussed during the meeting. He spoke in advance of the bilateral meeting with Xi about working together to end the fentanyl crisis.

▪ The Washington Post : Trump’s dream of nuclear deal meets unwilling Russia, China.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is aiming to make a decision by this morning on whether Republicans will move forward with a budget reconciliation bill to fund the Pentagon, a process that would be time-consuming. Thune has said Republicans would need to pass a budget resolution before Thanksgiving if they are to unlock the reconciliation process.

A scheduled vote to advance the nomination of Jim O’Neill to lead the National Science Foundation was called off after the Senate Health Committee’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), said O’Neill hadn’t done enough to “stand up for science.” The move comes a day after the White House withdrew Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid bipartisan scrutiny.

GOP Rep. Nick Begich is projected to win a second term representing Alaska’s sole House district following the completion of ranked-choice tabulation, according to Decision Desk HQ. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, left, and Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton, before the House Homeland Security Committee, Nov. 18, 2026, on Capitol Hill in Washington. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press)

TECH THREATS: Top administration officials sought to reassure lawmakers that there was no evidence that the recent technology outages were a result of nefarious activity or a coordinated attack at an annual hearing on worldwide threats facing the nation.

“The American people should ask us these questions,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes.”

“They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack,” Clayton added.

Clayton and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin were grilled for three hours before the House panel by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle who were not fully convinced that there was no connection between the various incidents, including outages affecting Microsoft, United Airlines, the National Security Agency, the Federal Aviation Administration and some of the country’s biggest banks.

“Five major disruptions in less than a week. Five different explanations,” Rep. Nick LaLota (R-N.Y.) said, before asking Clayton if his “gut” tells him that they are a coincidence.

“It does, and let me tell you why,” Clayton responded. “It’s an informed opinion, and the reason it’s informed is we are engaged in a substantial increase in upgrades, the number of patches, the number of upgrades that we’re undertaking in the public and private.”

ONE STEP CLOSER : House Democrats nominated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to be the next House Speaker, bringing him one step closer to making history as the first Black lawmaker to wield the gavel.

Jeffries ran uncontested, and the vote tally came to 251-11. That gives him a comfortable cushion ahead of Jan. 3, when his nomination heads to the floor for a full House vote and he’ll need 218 votes to officially win the Speakership.

Lawmakers were free to cast their votes anonymously, but a bloc of seven incoming members of Congress — including five backed by the Democratic Socialists of America — issued a joint statement making their “no” votes known. They said they were still looking for commitments from Jeffries on a number of progressive issues, including “Medicare for All,” U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the war in Gaza.

The party also chose Jeffries’s top deputies, Reps. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) and Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), as its choices for House majority leader and whip, respectively.

HEATING UP : Strikes from the U.S. and Iran are on the rise following a period of relative calm over the past two months.

Iran targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launched several attacks against Bahrain on Wednesday. Both countries said they were able to repel the attacks. These are the latest iteration in a series of tit-for-tat strikes between the U.S. and Tehran as Iran faces steep economic challenges as a result of the U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran previously tried to hit targets in Bahrain on Friday and Sunday, which the U.S. said were also intercepted. The U.S. conducted its own strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Tuesday, targeting an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps missile launch site, the second attack on the island this month.

Trump has said the war is “effectively over” but hasn’t ruled out resuming major combat operations.

CLOSER TIES : Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the U.S. and Venezuela have signed a deal to increase their military ties to counter foreign actors and “narco-terrorists.”

Hegseth made the announcement during an unannounced trip to the South American country, where he met with interim President Delcy Rodríguez in Caracas. The deal will allow the U.S. and Venezuela to conduct joint training and share intelligence.

The U.S. has moved increasingly close to Venezuela over the past year since its removal of former leader Nicolás Maduro in January, even as much of Maduro’s regime remains intact.

CAPITOL CRYPTO FORUM : Lawmakers, industry leaders and The Hill’s journalists convene today for a conference today focused on the state of the cryptocurrency industry and the push for implementing new regulations.

The forum will explore questions such as what the major hurdles are to a national regulatory framework and what’s next for crypto legislation currently in Congress. The series of panels and discussions will aim to bridge the gap between Capitol Hill and the crypto ecosystem.

FUNDING FIGHT : The Trump administration’s request for $50 billion for a new air traffic control system was at the center of the debate at The Hill’s “Red, Flight & Blue: Future of U.S. Aviation” event Wednesday.

During the conference, Federal Aviation Administration head Bryan Bedford took the blame for the agency’s ground stop that it issued for several hours on Friday. He maintained that the air traffic control system is “absolutely safe” but reiterated that the $50 billion is needed to modernize it.

Lawmakers at the event were mostly skeptical the request, demanding answers on what happened and how the additional funds will prevent it from happening again in the future.

“When they come and say they want $50 billion, and they say it’s Congress’s fault for not giving them the money, that’s not a really good way to begin the negotiation,” said Rep. Dina Titus (D-Nev.), a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Aviation.

GOP Rep. Steve Womack (R-Ark.) said he wants a “sequential plan” and “granular data” from the administration on why its funding request increased from $30 billion to $50 billion.

“We are, what, five days removed from a situation that really turned the country upside down. … I’m not satisfied that we have a complete forensics analysis and a satisfactory conclusion as to exactly what happened,” he told Sarah.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) suggested she isn’t opposed to the funding, but it must come with “accountability” for how the administration spends it.

At the same time, multiple aviation experts warned about the impacts a possible government shutdown next month would have on the industry. Airports have been among the most high-profile aspects of the economy impacted when the government shuts down.

“You’re going to tell me you’re not going to pay your own air traffic controllers and your TSA [Transportation Security Administration] officers and all of that as we’re going into the holidays?” said Chris Sununu , the president of Airlines for America and former New Hampshire governor, adding that he’s confident “common sense will prevail.”

CHANGING TIDES : A new study projects that Muslims will become the world’s largest religious group by 2035, marking the first time in centuries that Christians won’t hold the distinction.

The Pew Research Center report released Wednesday notes that both Islam and Christianity are growing in size, but Islam is growing faster. If current trends continue, the number of Muslims is expected to top 3.6 billion by 2070, while the number of Christians will be just short of 3 billion.

That would be an increase of 80 percent for Muslims and 30 percent for Christians.

Pew notes in its analysis that the expected changes are heavily influenced by demographic trends in the countries and regions where the religions are concentrated. Most of the world’s growth throughout the 21st century is expected to happen in Africa, especially sub-Saharan Africa, where most people are Christian or Muslim.

Differences in fertility also explain the projections, as Muslims tend to have more children than other religious groups.

The trend is also expected to take place in the U.S., though it’s projected to take longer. Christians are expected to lose their majority of the country by 2065, falling from two-thirds of the population in 2020.

Christianity will still remain the largest religion in the U.S. The shift is a result of an expected decline of Christians and a simultaneous increase in the number of people who don’t identify with any religion.

Meanwhile, the Jewish and Buddhist populations in North America are also expected to decline because of low fertility rates and relatively high median ages.

articles.title: Republicans hold lone Alaska House seat despite losing Senate, governor races
articles.summary: Rep. Nick Begich won re-election to Alaska's lone House seat after ranked-choice tabulation, a rare Republican bright spot in a Democratic wave.
articles.body: Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, won re-election to Alaska’s lone House seat Wednesday, surviving a Democratic wave that flipped both the Senate seat and the governor’s mansion. Begich, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated independent challenger Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and retired teacher backed by the Alaska Democratic Party, following the state’s ranked-choice voting tabulation. Begich’s victory, called at 9:27 p.m. ET on Wednesday – more than two weeks after Election Day – stood in sharp contrast to the rest of Alaska’s top-of-the-ticket results, where voters handed Democrats major breakthroughs despite Trump winning the state by 13% in 2024. HUNDREDS OF SUBPOENAS FLY IN DOJ’S ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE AS DEMOCRAT PELTOLA DECLARED WINNER IN ALASKA The race was among the final House contests called nationally after the Nov. 3 general election, offering a rare bright spot for Republicans in a midterm cycle that saw Democrats seize control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats thus far hold a 257-172 majority in the House, having flipped 46 seats to just three for Republicans. There are three races that remain too close to call. "This process requires engagement, and the perspectives brought forward during the campaign added value for Alaskans as they made important decisions about their vote in this race," Begich said in a statement after his victory. Hill, who campaigned on lowering costs, curbing big money in politics and pushing back against billionaires, said he called Begich to concede and congratulate him. "I wished him well as he continues representing Alaska in Congress, because all Alaskans have a stake in his success," Hill said in a statement. ALASKA DEM PELTOLA DEFEATS SULLIVAN, FLIPPING 9TH GOP SENATE SEAT AFTER 'DECOY DAN' UPROAR One day before Begich’s race was called, Democrat Mary Peltola unseated second-term Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. Peltola — who previously represented Alaska in the U.S. House before losing to Begich in 2024 — became the first Alaska native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the state in nearly two decades. Her victory cemented a 56-44 Democratic Senate majority, the party's largest since 2009. "As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola wrote on X. Democrats also secured the Alaska governor’s office for the first time in nearly 30 years, with Democrat Jonathan S. Kreiss-Tomkins winning the open-seat race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy. Throughout the House campaign, Begich pitched himself as an effective advocate aligned with Trump’s push to expand oil, gas and resource development in Alaska. But the final stretch of the race was overshadowed by controversy surrounding Democrat Eric Hafner, a perennial candidate with no ties to Alaska who is currently serving a sentence in a federal prison in New York following a 2022 conviction for threatening to kill judges, police officers and others. PELTOLA SAYS ALASKA ‘VOTED FOR CHANGE’ IN SENATE RACE Hafner, whose state election booklet biography made no mention of his incarceration, captured nearly 8% of the first-round vote. In the closing weeks of the race, Hill’s campaign distributed stickers and yard signs branding Hafner a "fake ‘Democrat,’" while state party officials spent thousands of dollars on text messages to clarify that Hill was the party’s endorsed candidate after mysterious, unsourced texts circulated promoting Hafner. Hafner’s mother, Carol "Kitty" Hafner — who also lacks ties to Alaska and finished sixth in the state's August Senate primary — dismissed claims that her son was recruited as a spoiler, writing in an email to The Associated Press that his runs have been "entirely independent of any influencers" and adding, "Tell President Trump to Pardon Eric Hafner!" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Controversy over alleged ballot spoilers also marked the Senate race, where independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan Jr. drew suspicion due to sharing a name with the Republican incumbent. Following reports that members of Peltola’s team helped recruit Sullivan Jr. into the race, the U.S. Justice Department opened a criminal investigation and Gov. Dunleavy ordered a state inquiry. Peltola has repeatedly denied any involvement. "I personally know that I am innocent, so I don’t spend a lot of time hand-wringing" about it, Peltola said Wednesday. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: On the Ballot: Democrats’ huge freshman class has bigger plans than passing an agenda
articles.summary: The incoming class of House freshmen are already plotting how to shake up and shape up Congress in the coming weeks. Just two weeks since their historic elections, new House Democrats want to pass big-ticket agenda items like reversing Medicaid cuts and banning members from trading stocks as some of the first priorities in one…
articles.body:
The incoming class of House freshmen are already plotting how to shake up and shape up Congress in the coming weeks.

Just two weeks since their historic elections, new House Democrats want to pass big-ticket agenda items like reversing Medicaid cuts and banning members from trading stocks as some of the first priorities in one of the party’s largest majorities in Congress in recent memory.

But the new freshmen Democrats – whose resumes include smokejumper, mayor, state lawmaker and emergency nurse – are also eager to change the culture in and around Washington, D.C., looking to make it more reflective of the people who helped usher them into office and leaning into bipartisanship.

“I want to see, frankly, more of what I am happy to see in our freshman class, like just normal working people who are in the halls here,” Rep.-elect Sam Forstag (D-Mont.), a smokejumper and union leader, told The Hill. “It is far too rare a thing for a working-class person to make it up here nowadays, and that is a fundamental issue of representation, as I see it.”

The new class of Democratic House freshmen are set to enter their largest majority since at least 2008, the last time the party held at least 257 seats in the lower chamber. But with some House races still uncalled by Decision Desk HQ, House Democrats may see the kinds of numbers they last saw in the 1990s.

In 1992, Democrats held 258 seats in the lower chamber, though it may be harder to top the 1990 cycle, when the party won 267 seats.

More than half of the American labor force consider themselves working-class, but lawmakers with that background — manual labor, service industry and clerical jobs — make up just 2 percent of Congress.

The majority of Congress were millionaires for the first time in 2014. Nearly three-quarters of the current senators now hit that benchmark.

The incoming Congress changes those numbers, after 17 union members won their races this month.

Running for Congress is “a really big ask for even a well-situated person,” Nicholas Carnes , a public policy professor at Duke who has studied working-class representation in government, said. “But for a working-class person who has a job that’s maybe a little more precarious, who doesn’t have a lot of savings, who can’t afford to just like upend their lives to take a chance on politics. That’s going to be an impossible ask for a lot of working-class people.”

Some members are seeing that disconnect in real time.

“You can tell we’ve had a long history of wealthy people being elected because that’s really the way a lot of it’s set up, from the way you secure your housing and get transported — most of the stuff is not covered by the government,” Rep.-elect Cyril Jefferson (D-N.C.), the current mayor of High Point, N.C., told The Hill.

“You got to pay for it personally. Campaign funds can’t pay for a lot of things, and so I only share that because I think we’ve got a ways to go to truly get our government back to where it’s a government of common people,” he added.

Inversely, it makes it harder for Congress to advocate for issues on the minds of working-class voters if too few are represented in the chambers, Carnes said.

“Politicians bring their whole life experiences with them to office, and when you don’t have people with life experience in working class jobs, your institutions don’t have access to the information they need to really represent the interests of workers,” Carnes said.

The burden of campaigning itself is one major hurdle for the working-class candidate, according to Carnes. On top of the personal risks that plague any candidate, working-class people are more likely than professional counterparts to say they’re worried about taking time off or paying bills along the campaign trail. That could also lead major party players and interest groups to favor white-collar candidates instead.

Rep.-elect Matt Little (D-Minn.), a former state senator and attorney, said one of the biggest things that’s surprised him about running for Congress has been the amount of time he had to dedicate to fundraising.

“The speeches and the in-person stuff is so — such a small part of congressional campaigning. It’s all on the phone trying to raise money,” Little said. “That’s the bulk of it, and we’ve got to change that, too.”

“You can’t accurately represent people if all you do all day is call people that can give you $1,000 or more,” he added.

Some groups, like the New Jersey AFL-CIO’s “Labor Candidates School,” are trying to give working-class candidates the tools they need to run. Carnes and other researchers have also proposed seed money programs for workers, targeted political scholarships and reserved party leadership seats for working-class people as potential reforms.

This year’s midterms also elected a historically diverse slate of candidates that increases representation across key demographic blocs.

A record-breaking 155 women are set to serve in the 120th Congress, or nearly a third of Capitol Hill – representing 51 percent of the country.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) is the first Muslim American elected to the Senate. Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) will be the first Native American woman in the Senate. A record three Black women will serve in the Senate at the same time. And as Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso (R-Wisc.), age 26, becomes the youngest person in the House, incoming senators are nearly 15 years younger, on average, than departing ones.

The new freshmen are taking different approaches to how to shake up the culture in Congress and around Washington, D.C.

“I don’t know anything about the culture before that I’m stepping into, but what I’ll say is the perception is there’s not a lot of bipartisanship. I would like to change that,” Rep.-elect Zach Dembo (D-Ky.), a former federal prosecutor and former Navy JAG officer, told The Hill. “I just organized a little informal bipartisan mixer yesterday with like 10 of us because so many of us were saying we wish we had a chance to talk across the aisle, so I’d like to do a lot more of that.”

Little, from Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, said that he wanted to prove to voters that candidates can be consistent between what they campaign on in their home states and back in Washington, D.C.

“You don’t have to get sucked into the culture or the money, and you can do exactly what you said on the campaign trail here,” the Minnesota Democrat said.

In addition to looking for more working-class representation in Congress, Forstag quipped “we can start with the ties” when asked how he was personally looking to shake up the culture in Congress.

Jefferson, meanwhile, said he wanted lawmakers to lean into compassion while having difficult conservations.

“We can take the political fight where we need to take it, while also making sure that we don’t lose our humanity and our decency in the process,” he said.

Welcome to The Hill’s On The Ballot. We’re Julia Mueller and Caroline Vakil — reach out to us on X ( @jmthewriter + @CarolineVakil) or via email ( jmueller@thehill.com + cvakil@thehill.com.)

An inside look at Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s winning strategy in Mississippi.

Few campaigns have amassed as much attention this cycle as Sen.-elect Scott Colom ’s (D) shocking upset against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) in Mississippi.

While the Colom campaign has become synonymous with the “Pick Another Protein” ad — in which the Mississippi Democrat mocks Hyde-Smith for suggesting voters can enjoy other sources of protein while beef prices are still high – his brother, Andrew Colom , told On The Ballot that the reception to their content didn’t necessarily start out positive.

“We’re doing ads after ads after ads for a year and a half, and … the DC consultants were definitely saying, ‘You guys are doing too many ads,’ but they were definitely wrong,” Andrew Colom said. “I mean, definitely all the ads we were doing, not only were they refining our skills, but they were just always tripling down our message.”

Colom, a filmmaker and co-founder and chairman of the investment and real estate company Century Partners, told On The Ballot that their ads had received some traction earlier on during the campaign, including one where the senator-elect visits a grocery store in Hyde-Smith’s hometown and notes the prices of chicken, pork and catfish are expensive.

“It sho is,” a woman working in the grocery store’s meat department tells the camera each time.

The attention early on from MS NOW anchor Symone Sanders and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) also felt like a key turning point in the campaign, Andrew Colom said.

Another ad Sen.-elect Scott Colom’s campaign did that attracted attention was one based off the 2025 “Sinners” movie , which is set in the Mississippi Delta during the 1930s. Andrew and Scott Colom, identical twin brothers, repurpose the roles of “Smoke” and “Stake” while treating Hyde-Smith as the ad’s “vampire.”

Andrew Colom said they spent a total of $4,000 on the ad.

“I remember that iconic image of Michael B. Jordan handing himself a cigarette on the smoking stack [that] I think became either the cover or one of the defining images of the artwork, so I was like, ‘Oh, you know what, I could do it instead of a cigarette,’” Andrew Colom said. “’I’ll pass him a brochure, and he can then pass it to the camera and … tell the camera, ‘We can do it together.’”
