articles.title: Florida Christians rebel against Imam's prayer opening a city meeting with a message of their own
articles.summary: Christian protesters reciting the Lord's Prayer interrupted Imam Sajid Bhuiya's invocation at a Bartow, Florida meeting before police stepped in.
articles.body: An imam who was scheduled to deliver the invocation at a city commission meeting Monday evening in a southwest Florida town was interrupted by Christian protesters — who had a prayer of their own to share. Footage from inside the meeting obtained by Fox News Digital shows dozens of Christian activists crowded into the back of a Bartow, Florida city commission meeting room. As Imam Sajid Bhuiya of the town's Masjid Al-Nur Mosque stepped up to the lectern to give the invocation, they began reciting the Lord's Prayer in unison. Some chants of "USA!" broke out, as well. According to Robert Goodman, the southeast regional director of the conservative activist group Citizens Defending Freedom, news of Bhuiya's scheduled appearance began making the rounds on social media last weekend. He was among those who shared the news on social media. Goodman said about 100 people from different groups ended up attending the meeting. IOWA CITY COUNCIL MEETING ERUPTS AFTER FORMER MEMBER OPENS WITH SATANIC PRAYER AND 'HAIL SATAN' "Citizens Defending Freedom believes Christian voices deserve to be heard on matters affecting our communities, families, and freedoms, which is why we joined many other concerned citizens and organizations Monday night," Goodman told Fox News Digital. He said the Quran teaches forced submission and permits men to strike their wives, while viewing the opinions of women as lesser than the opinions of men. "We have every right to challenge teachings we believe conflict with human dignity, equality, religious liberty and America's founding principles, because we must be intolerant of intolerance while respecting every person's right to believe differently," he said. Video from the city's official livestream of the event quickly went viral online. PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH' Some protesters made off-color comments, including telling Bhuiya to go back to his own country, which Goodman clarified that neither he nor his organization support. "The disrespectful remarks made by two or three individuals Monday night do not represent me or Citizens Defending Freedom, because as Christians, we are called to speak truth with conviction and respect, not insults," Goodman said. Goodman said Bhuiya was invited to deliver the invocation by a city official. Members of the commission mostly sat quietly, observing the commotion while police handled the crowd. Police eventually escorted the Christian protesters out of the building, though no arrests were made. Bhuiya then spoke, quoting passages from the Quran that he said are meant to unify people. "This is a reminder that our differences in background, culture and faiths should not prevent us from treating one another with dignity," he said. Fox News Digital reached out to the Masjid Al-Nur Mosque for comment on the disruption of Bhuiya's invocation. SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT The city of Bartow released a statement explaining the Imam's appearance at the meeting. The statement said that residents, "joined by individuals from other cities, attempted to prevent the imam from speaking and the Mayor from proceeding to conduct the business at hand." "For years, it has been tradition to open Bartow City Commission meetings with a prayer offered by either a faith-based leader or one of the City's elected officials," it said. "While historically the opening invocation/prayer is one based on Christian traditions, the opportunity is open to all faiths. This is consistent with the United States Constitution." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In the statement, city officials called for residents, "including religious leaders of all faiths, to come together to ensure that Bartow continues to be a welcoming place for all who live, work and play in Polk County's capital city."

articles.title: Wife of American wrongfully detained in China calls for his release after Trump-Xi meeting
articles.summary: Sylvia Zin says her U.S. citizen husband Min Zin is held in solitary confinement in China without legal counsel, after Trump met with Xi Jinping again.
articles.body: The wife of U.S. citizen Min Zin, whom the State Department has declared "wrongfully detained" in China, issued a fresh call for his release Thursday after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping. "It has now been nearly six months since my husband, Min Zin, a United States citizen and independent academic, was lured to China and wrongfully detained," Sylvia Zin said in a statement. "My husband is being held by the Chinese government on false charges at an undisclosed location in solitary confinement without any access to legal counsel," she added. "We have no idea why they detained him and why they continue to hold him." "This is the second in-person meeting that President Trump has held with Chinese President Xi since Min Zin was arrested. I am grateful for the President's commitment in continuing to raise my husband's wrongful detention and his work to secure Min Zin's immediate and unconditional release," Sylvia Zin also said. "My daughter and I remain hopeful in the President's ability to bring him home to us in time for the holidays." TRUMP, PUTIN, XI ISSUE 4-POINT DECLARATION AFTER HISTORIC SUMMIT When asked Thursday to respond to Sylvia Zin's statement, a White House official told Fox News Digital that Trump cares deeply about the return of Americans being held abroad and has brought home more than 100 from around the globe. The State Department said in August that Secretary of State Marco Rubio determined Zin was "wrongfully detained" following an extensive review "of the circumstances surrounding his June 3 detention in Yunnan, China, where Mr. Zin had traveled to attend an academic conference at the invitation of the Chinese government." TRUMP TO ASK XI TO FREE WRONGFULLY DETAINED US CITIZEN AS WIFE SPEAKS OUT "There are now two wrongfully detained U.S. citizens in China: Mr. Zin and Dr. Youlin Chen," Assistant Secretary Dylan Johnson said at the time. "The safety and security of U.S. citizens is the State Department’s top priority. We will continue to advocate for Mr. Zin and call for the release of all U.S. citizens who are arbitrarily detained or exit-banned in China." China's Foreign Ministry claimed Zin was arrested in June on suspicion of spying and endangering national security, according to Reuters. The Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar think tank said Zin is its director, and The Associated Press reported in June that Zin was a Ph.D. candidate at the University of California, Berkeley. Sylvia Zin also said in her statement, "We recently learned that Min Zin was hospitalized last month for severe dehydration due to stomach illness and that there is no heat in the location he is being held. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I try to remain strong for our daughter," she added, "but my worry for my husband's health and well-being grows unbearably with each passing day." Fox News' Nicholas Kalman and Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

articles.title: Classified NSA network is still down, leaving some staff working from home
articles.summary: The network went down on Tuesday due to a technical problem during maintenance operations, but sources say it has not affected its work collecting electronic intelligence.
articles.body: An internal classified computer network used by the National Security Agency remained down on Thursday, resulting in some employees being ordered to work from home for a third day in a row, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. The network first went down on Tuesday due to a technical problem that occurred when maintenance on the network was underway. Both sources told NBC News the issue has created an inconvenience but has not affected the NSA’s work collecting electronic intelligence around the world and overseeing cybersecurity. There is no sign that the outage was caused by a cyberattack, the sources said. Even though the NSA’s network issue came amid an unusual series of mass outages that have wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails over the past few days, U.S. officials have said say there is no indication that the technical problems were caused by a coordinated cyberattack. Nonessential staff at the NSA are being told to check in with their supervisors and find out if they need to come into the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland. Otherwise, they are advised to work from home, according to a telephone information line for the workforce and the two sources familiar with the matter. While the NSA does not release the precise number of agency employees, former officials have said it employs tens of thousands of people. In 2024, a Maryland state government document put the number of NSA employees at 39,000. The agency has since made some workforce reductions as part of broader cutbacks across the federal government. The outage also affected a worksite in Georgia that handles the NSA’s electronic intelligence work in the Middle East, the sources said. In a statement Tuesday, the NSA acknowledged experiencing a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the statement said. “NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” The NSA, which oversees the nation’s vast electronic surveillance efforts, is considered one of the world’s most sophisticated cybersecurity and electronic spy agencies. With powerful eavesdropping and code-breaking tools as well as a well-educated workforce, the NSA prides itself as a center of digital expertise. While it is not uncommon for government networks to suffer brief disruptions or outages, such a high-profile technical problem threatens to tarnish the reputation the agency has built, according to former officials and experts.

articles.title: Dems, GOP rebels fail to rein in Trump's Iran war in Senate, but bigger battle looms
articles.summary: Senate Democrats and rebel Republicans fail to pass a war powers resolution over Trump's Iran war, as Tim Kaine denies Republican shutdown threats.
articles.body: Senate Democrats failed to peel off enough Republicans to rebuke President Donald Trump and his war against Iran as another battle looms on the horizon. In the first attempt after the midterm elections, Democrats and the squadron of rebel Republicans, including Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Rand Paul, R-Ky., were not enough to pass a non-binding resolution that originally passed the House, pushed by Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., in September. Like the previous war powers resolutions, this effort would have required the removal of troops engaged in hostilities not authorized by Congress in the region. Even if it had passed, it was a more symbolic move given that it was non-binding and would not have been sent to Trump’s desk. DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN But in the background, Senate Democrats are eyeing another battleground to be more forceful with their desire to rein in the war: government funding. The deadline to either fully fund or extend current funding is Dec. 11. Senate Republicans have warned that their counterparts intend to use the process as a cudgel to stymie tax dollars meant for the war and are willing to shut down the government to do so. "I'm increasingly concerned that the Democrats may try to initiate another, a third government shutdown this year," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "And that would be a terrible outcome for the American people and something I hope that they will think better of." CHRIS VAN HOLLEN FLOATS USING GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN THREAT TO FORCE TRUMP TO END IRAN WAR Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., countered to Fox News Digital that Senate Republicans were the ones who wanted to "shut the government down to maintain an illegal war that has just been massively repudiated by the American public." "We're gonna fund government in a robust way. We're gonna fund the defense in a robust way, but if they say, ‘Yeah, that's not enough, we have to be able to continue a war that's illegal, and the American public hates,’ that'll be on them, not on us," Kaine said. "We're not gonna shut government down." Thune’s comments came as Republicans were, until Wednesday afternoon, considering taking defense funding off the table and ramming a $350 billion request from the administration through with the budget reconciliation process. But after a marathon closed-door meeting with Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg, Republicans opted to give a shot at bipartisanship. SENATE REPUBLICANS PLAN 54-DAY BLITZ TO PUSH TRUMP'S AGENDA BEFORE DEMOCRATS SEIZE POWER "I think the consensus of the conference is, you know, there are downsides to reconciliation," Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said. "We're not giving up by any means, but we would like to give Democrats a chance to work through an appropriations process, defense supplemental, that kind of stuff." Senate Democrats acknowledged that they’re in a hard spot when it comes to the funding back and forth, with some recognizing that they need to agree to funding the Pentagon and restocking munitions while struggling to find the balancing act on guardrails against taxpayer dollars flowing to the war effort. "We're in a really tough place," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., said. "I've been saying for months that the war with Iran has no support in my caucus. We are searching for responsible ways to bring it to an end, and a supplemental is a nonstarter, a reconciliation bill is a nonstarter, but I recognize we also need to find ways to invest in and support our troops and our security." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Republicans are also cautiously optimistic that Democrats will play ball, given the recent history with two record-shattering government shutdowns. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., was more optimistic than some of his colleagues, and told Fox News Digital that "I've got a lot of Democrat friends, both on the Armed Services Committee, who are, who are very supportive of our military. [They] understand the threat in the world." "You know, they may have to, they may have to swallow their ‘I hate Trump pride’ a little bit, but, at the end of the day, there are a lot of people that are convincible," Cramer said. "But it does require talking to them. You know?"

articles.title: ‘On the same page’: Hegseth hails US ties with Colombia’s de la Espriella
articles.summary: The US defence secretary praised security cooperation with Colombia as country joins Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.
articles.body:
Bogota, Colombia – United States Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has hailed the White House’s close alliance with far-right Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella during a brief visit to the capital, Bogota.

The US envoy met with top officials on Wednesday to discuss cooperation against organised crime and drug trafficking in the region.

They also announced Colombia as the likely host of next year’s meeting of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (AC3).

“It was an excellent meeting, and we’re completely on the same page. And I think the reason we’re on the same page is because both of our countries are led by strong, clear leaders,” Hegseth told reporters on Wednesday.

The US defence secretary landed at an Air Force base in Bogota around 1pm local time (18:00 GMT) Wednesday, before having a closed-door meeting with Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Mora and the General Commander of the Armed Forces Erik Rodriguez.

The military leaders discussed the difficulties of combatting the armed groups active in Colombia, particularly along the border with Venezuela , and the mounting challenge posed by their use of advanced drones, according to local media reports.

De la Espriella, a political outsider, was elected on a promise to crush Colombia’s cartels through military force. Sergio Guzman, director of Colombia Risk Analysis, a political risk consultancy, said the president will require US support to achieve his goals.

“Colombia’s fiscal situation suggests that the government needs as much assistance as it can get,” argued the analyst.

Though no new funding commitments materialised during the visit, Hegseth presided over the formal delivery of a Lockheed C-130 Hercules plane, used to transport troops and cargo, to the Colombian Air Force.

“We’ve partnered more deeply with Colombia than ever before, and now we are just enhancing that cooperation and that partnership,” Hegseth told reporters.

Standing next to Hegseth at a news conference, Mora also announced that Colombia would host next year’s meeting of the AC3, also known as the Shield of the Americas.

Launched in March, the AC3 serves as an alliance of US-aligned nations in Latin America and the Caribbean, aimed at combatting organised crime through a military-centred approach.

Colombia only recently joined the coalition when de la Espriella – who was endorsed by Trump – took power in August, replacing leftist Gustavo Petro, who regularly clashed with the White House.

The Trump administration has been pressuring members of the alliance to allow US strikes on their territory, as it seeks to expand its bombing campaign against suspected drug vessels in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific to land operations.

Though Hegseth announced at an August AC3 summit in Panama that de la Espriella had authorised joint military operations, The New York Times reported yesterday that the Colombian president had since shot down the idea of direct US intervention in Colombia.

The New York Times also reported that Hegseth shortened his visit to Colombia as a result of the rejection of a bilateral military agreement.

Both Hegseth and de la Espriella described the report as “false”, highlighting ongoing close collaboration between the two militaries.

But de la Espriella noted that the move would require congressional approval, something that would be difficult, given unfavourable public opinion.

Guzman noted that Colombia’s rejection of direct US strikes likely deals a blow to the White House’s hopes for direct intervention against drug traffickers.

“Colombia is at the centre, the keystone of the strategy. So that’s quite a disappointment for [the Trump administration], I can imagine,” he said.

Hegseth also visited Venezuela on Wednesday, where he signed a bilateral deal pledging US military support for Caracas. He later departed Colombia for Ecuador and is also scheduled to make a brief stop in Honduras.

articles.title: Americans could face $100 hike in internet bills under plan eyed by lawmakers
articles.summary: Sens. Deb Fischer and Ben Ray Luján drafted a bill that would add up to $100 to people's internet bills to fund the Universal Service Fund.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A bipartisan group of lawmakers is eyeing adding a tax to internet usage throughout the country to help subsidize telecommunications services in rural areas. Sens. Deb Fischer, R-Neb., and Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., have quietly been working on draft legislation that would add up to $100 extra on Americans’ internet bills to bolster the Universal Service Fund (USF), a decades-old program meant to subsidize broadband access, a source shared with Fox News Digital. Fischer and Luján formed a bipartisan and bicameral working group for USF reform last year with Reps. Doris Matsui, D-Calif., and Richard Hudson, R-N.C. to find fixes for the program, which was first launched in 1996. FCC LAUNCHES SWEEPING REVIEW OF $3B SCHOOL INTERNET SUBSIDY PROGRAM OVER SCREEN TIME CONCERNS The draft legislation, which has yet to be officially filed in the Senate and is still subject to change, included proposals to create a USF tax on households and businesses with broadband connections. The draft legislation, which was reviewed by Fox News Digital, would also increase the current USF tax on cell phone lines and impose no cap on USF spending — meaning there’s wiggle room to raise the tax down the line. "I’m not commenting on gossip intended to undermine USF reform, particularly when a bill hasn’t even been filed," Fischer said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Another source familiar with the negotiations around the yet-to-be revealed legislation told Fox News Digital that they had "no reason to believe" that the fee had been removed from the draft bill. "My understanding is it just adds a tax on broadband," they said. Congress does not directly fund the program, which instead relies on user fees from telecommunications and broadband companies to stay afloat in order to subsidize broadband services in rural areas. FCC CHAIRMAN CARR SAYS SPECTRUM AUCTION WILL MAKE WIRELESS FASTER, CHEAPER WHILE RAISING BILLIONS FOR TREASURY Last year, according to data from the Congressional Research Service, the USF doled out over $8 billion in subsidies. Part of the problem with the program is that the stream of funding that props USF up is shrinking, according to a report from the Computer & Communications Industry Association. The report found that "the current contribution base for USF fell 41% between the first quarter of 2018 and the first quarter of 2026, from $12.9 billion to $7.6 billion." That is spurred by shifts in the industry and contribution base, like more communications happening over the internet through WhatsApp, FaceTime and Zoom instead of phone calls, for example. And tacking on a new tax to bolster the program is a touchy subject, particularly for outside groups. TOP SENATE DEM’S NEW TAX IDEA GETS TORCHED AS CRITICS WARN NEARLY EVERY AMERICAN COULD PAY Over two dozen outside groups led by Grover Norquist’s Americans for Tax Reform demanded in a letter to Congress sent in August that lawmakers "oppose any attempts to impose new taxes on broadband service, including by assessing broadband for contributions" to the USF. "Rather than impose new taxes on broadband providers, raising costs yet further for consumers, Congress should reform eligibility for the program and retire the broadband subsidies, if not the entire program," they wrote. "USF is outdated and ill-suited for its purpose. Passing off its ballooning costs is not a solution." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Congress did enact a new infrastructure-expansion focused internet program under former President Joe Biden in 2021 as part of his Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. That program, called the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD), included a one-time pot of just over $42 billion to spread internet access across the country. The Trump administration overhauled the program, removing hurdles and adding new guidelines for states and territories to gain access to the funding. Fox News Digital reached out to Luján’s office for comment.

articles.title: Trump ally Bill Essayli tapped to lead investigation of Biden officials over Mar-a-Lago raid
articles.summary: Bill Essayli will probe whether Biden officials broke the law in the FBI's 2022 raid on Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate, which sparked Jack Smith's case.
articles.body: A California federal prosecutor embroiled in a legal battle over his own authority is heading to Florida to investigate the FBI’s 2022 raid on President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate. Two sources familiar with the investigation confirmed to Fox News Digital that First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli will serve as a special assistant tasked with investigating whether Biden Justice Department officials broke federal law when executing their search warrant on Mar-a-Lago. Essayli will continue to hold his position as first assistant U.S. attorney, splitting his time between Florida and Los Angeles, a source familiar said. Essayli’s inquiry into the Mar-a-Lago search, which initiated former special counsel Jack Smith’s classified documents case, is a part of a broader Justice Department probe. Attorney General Pam Bondi initially launched the "grand conspiracy" investigation in August 2025 to target Obama-era officials, but its scope has since expanded to examine allegations that Biden officials also conspired to unlawfully prosecute Trump. Essayli is the latest prosecutor tapped to oversee the investigation after the resignations of two other attorneys in the past few months. Just a few weeks ago, Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, resigned abruptly. His departure came two months after he took over from Joe diGenova, a lawyer selected by Attorney General Todd Blanche to supervise the investigation who resigned in September. PROSECUTOR JOSEPH DIGENOVA RESIGNS FROM DOJ ROLE INVESTIGATING TRUMP-RUSSIA PROBES DiGenova's resignation in September came just five months after he was tapped to oversee the investigation amid growing frustration within the White House and Justice Department over the lack of criminal charges. Fox News Digital previously reported that diGenova had effectively been sidelined before his departure, while sources told the New York Post he had lost the confidence of administration officials over concerns he was "slow-rolling" indictments and pursuing dead-end leads. Essayli's involvement in the inquiry adds another layer of controversy to the investigation for two reasons. TRUMP-FIRED US ATTORNEY LAUNCHES UNPRECEDENTED COURT FIGHT AFTER JUST 54 MINUTES ON THE JOB For one, Essayli's authority to lead the U.S. Attorney's Office in Los Angeles is already under judicial scrutiny. In October, U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright ruled that Essayli was unlawfully serving as a "de facto" U.S. attorney, finding that the Justice Department had effectively circumvented restrictions on temporary appointments by allowing him to continue exercising the powers of the office without Senate confirmation. Essayli was initially appointed interim U.S. attorney in April 2025, a position generally limited to 120 days. When that period expired, the Justice Department appointed him to other positions, including first assistant U.S. attorney, while allowing him to continue overseeing the office. Seabright concluded that changing Essayli's title did not resolve the underlying legal problem and disqualified him from supervising two criminal prosecutions. On Monday, the judge rejected the Justice Department's request to suspend that ruling while the government pursued an appeal. Although that decision does not automatically invalidate Essayli's separate assignment in Florida, it raises questions about his continuing authority in Los Angeles as he takes on another politically sensitive investigation. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Essayli's close ties to Trump have also drawn scrutiny from Democrats and defense attorneys over whether he can remain impartial in an investigation involving the president's political adversaries. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A former Republican California state lawmaker and vocal Trump supporter, Essayli has pledged to work "tirelessly" to carry out the administration's priorities at the Justice Department, prompting House Democrats led by Rep. Dave Min, D-Calif., to demand an ethics probe over alleged "politically-motivated investigations." Meanwhile, H. Dean Steward, a veteran Newport Beach federal defense attorney and former directing attorney of the Orange County Federal Public Defender Office who successfully challenged Essayli's authority in California, has accused the Trump administration of violating federal law "in an effort to install minions as chief federal prosecutors." Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Fox News' Jake Gibson and David Spunt contributed to this report.
